title: A Name Handed Down
hookLine: Ashkenazim often name after relatives who have died, Sephardim often after living grandparents
carry: a child's name carries a loved one forward

lines: A NAME FROM THE ONE WHO DIED.
A NAME FROM THE ONE IN THE FRONT ROW.
cards: Two families, two baby boys, the same week. In the first, the baby is named after his great-grandfather, who died last spring. When the name is announced, his grandmother starts to cry, and then to laugh.
In the second, the baby is named after his grandfather, who is standing right there in the front row, holding the camera and suddenly unable to work it.
Two customs, two very different moments, and underneath both, the same conviction.

teach.h: NAMED FOR THE ONES WHO DIED.
NAMED FOR THE ONES STILL HERE.
teach.b: Jews whose families come from Central and Eastern Europe have often named children after relatives who have died, and often avoided naming after anyone still living.
The name becomes a way to keep someone present: a grandmother who never met the baby is named aloud every time the child is called to dinner. Second, the Sephardi custom.
Jews whose families come from Spain, North Africa and the Middle East have often done the opposite: they name children after living grandparents.
To hear your own name given to a grandchild, while you're alive to hear it, is a great honor. One custom carries the dead forward. The other crowns the living.
Both say a child doesn't arrive from nowhere. Third, the old roots.

teach.h: LET MY NAME BE NAMED IN THEM.
teach.b: In Genesis, when Jacob blesses his grandsons, he asks that his own name, and the names of Abraham and Isaac, be named in them. Long before either custom, a grandfather wanted to live on in the children's names.
And Proverbs puts it plainly: "A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches." Fourth, the name you earn.
A midrash teaches that every person has three names: the one their parents give, the one other people call them, and the one they acquire for themselves, and the last is the best.
The family can hand down a name. Only a life can fill it.

how: Ashkenazi Jews often name a baby after a relative who has died, while Sephardi Jews often name children after living grandparents; the Hebrew name is announced at a brit milah or a naming for a girl.

games.q: you're in a Sephardi family, and a new grandson is about to be named. your father is in the front row. what does custom often suggest?
o: name the baby after your father, while he's alive to hear it.
choose a name nobody in the family has had.
wait until your father has died.
games.why: Sephardi families often name after living grandparents; hearing your name given to a grandchild is an honor.

practice: Say your own first name quietly, once, and ask what you know about it: who chose it, whether you were named for someone, what name they almost gave you instead.
If someone comes to mind, sit with them a moment; if you don't know, notice the question, and who might. Then think of the third name, the one you're earning, and what you'd want it to say.

wordCard.voice: Names carry people. Named for the dead, or for the living, and then filled by a life. Today's word.
